facts.title: Named After a Scottish Village
facts.text: Strontium is the only element named after a place in the United Kingdom: the village of Strontian (Sròn an t-Sìthein) in the Scottish Highlands. The mineral strontianite was first noticed in lead mines there in the 1790s. The pure metal was finally isolated in 1808 by Humphry Davy using electrolysis, the same technique he used to win several other elements that year.

facts.title: The Color of Red Fireworks
facts.text: Strontium salts such as strontium nitrate and strontium carbonate are the classic source of brilliant crimson-red in fireworks, flares, and emergency road signals. When heated, strontium atoms emit light strongly at wavelengths around 650-680 nanometers, producing one of the purest reds available to pyrotechnicians. This same red flame test is a quick laboratory way to confirm the presence of strontium.

facts.title: Twin of Calcium
facts.text: Strontium sits directly below calcium in Group 2 of the periodic table, so it behaves chemically very much like it. Because of this similarity, the body treats strontium like calcium and deposits roughly 99% of any absorbed strontium into bones and teeth. This biological mimicry is the key to both its medical uses and its dangers.

facts.title: The Fallout Isotope
facts.text: Strontium-90 is a radioactive isotope produced in nuclear fission, and it became infamous during 1950s atmospheric bomb testing. Because it mimics calcium, it lodges in growing bones, where its half-life of about 28.8 years means it can irradiate tissue for decades. Detecting Sr-90 in children's baby teeth helped build public pressure that led to the 1963 Partial Test Ban Treaty.

facts.title: A Battery for Spacecraft
facts.text: That same strontium-90 is actually useful as a power source, because its radioactive decay releases a steady stream of heat. Radioisotope thermoelectric generators fueled by Sr-90 once powered remote lighthouses, weather stations, and navigation beacons in the former Soviet Union. The heat is converted directly into electricity with no moving parts, allowing decades of unattended operation.

facts.title: Fighting Bone Cancer Pain
facts.text: The radioactive isotope strontium-89, sold as a chloride solution, is injected to ease the severe pain of cancer that has spread to the bones. Because strontium concentrates in bone, the isotope's beta radiation targets the tumor sites directly while sparing much of the body. It offers relief to patients whose pain no longer responds well to standard medication.

facts.title: Stronger Teeth and Bones
facts.text: In a non-radioactive form, strontium ranelate was prescribed in Europe to treat osteoporosis, because it both slows bone breakdown and modestly encourages new bone formation. Strontium chloride is also the active ingredient in some toothpastes marketed for sensitive teeth, where it helps block exposed nerve channels in dentine. These uses again exploit strontium's natural affinity for hard tissues.

facts.title: It Glows Through Old TVs
facts.text: For much of the 20th century, one of the largest industrial uses of strontium was in the glass faceplates of cathode-ray-tube televisions and monitors. Strontium oxide added to the glass absorbed harmful X-rays generated by the electron beam, protecting viewers. As flat-screen displays replaced bulky CRTs, this once-dominant market for strontium largely disappeared.

facts.title: Forged in Dying Stars
facts.text: Strontium is created in the cosmos mainly inside aging stars through slow neutron capture, the so-called s-process. In 2019, astronomers detected newly made strontium in the glowing debris of a neutron-star collision observed in 2017, the first clear identification of a specific heavy element from such a merger. This confirmed that violent stellar smashups help seed the universe with elements like strontium.

facts.title: A Clock Accurate to the Cosmos
facts.text: Atoms of strontium are at the heart of some of the most precise clocks ever built. Optical lattice clocks trap strontium atoms in a grid of laser light and measure an electron transition that ticks hundreds of trillions of times per second. The best strontium clocks are so stable they would neither gain nor lose a single second over many billions of years, longer than the current age of the universe.
